title: Computer victory at Go: a humantragedy
content:
1. AlphaGo, the computer, developed by artificial intelligence (AI) researchers at Google, won four victories to win a five-game match against Lee Se-dol, one of the world's best players of the game Go.

2. It wasn't supposed to ever be like this. Sure, the best computers have been able to defeat world chess champions for over a decade. But Go was supposed to be impossible to solve. Or at least not solvable so soon. AlphaGo beat the European champion in 2015, but he wasn't rated a top player. No big deal.

3. Go was safe, we thought, because Go was different. It's not just calculation. It's intuition. It's a creative act. It's a feeling for structure. It's a calm appreciation of space and shape and direction. In short, it's art.

4. The difficulty of Go has long contributed to its appeal. In the West in particular, the game has had an image of mystery. "Not one in a hundred Europeans living in Japan," commented a British player, "has taken the time needed to learn and appreciate the value of Go, or to enjoy playing the game."

5. My brother, a very skilled player, used to refer to Go as chess to the fourth power. It's often called the most perfect game of strategy ever invented. Most importantly, Go was supposed to be the game least likely to be broken by machines.

6. Don't get me wrong. I'm not anti-tech. I'm fascinated by AI. When I was at Stanford University back in the 1970s, the courses I took on the subject – in both computer science and philosophy – were among the most interesting and exciting of my college career. Yet I will admit that I am no trans-humanist. I like to imagine that there will remain areas of uniquely human effort. So, if the world of games has been conquered, what's left for humans to protect?

7. One possibility is the arts, often said to be such complex products of observation, experience, imagination and emotion that they take years or decades to master. But, no. Even in the arts, humans have been challenged by AI.

8. Take poetry. I remember the simple programs we came up with in high school and college. The IBM computer would groan and struggle and after hours of work produce something like this: DOWN BY THE BROWN HORSE VERILY / THE RED HOUSE SADDENED MERRILY. Now you can take an online challenge to figure out whether a poem was written by a computer or a human. Mostly you'll be able to tell, but it's getting harder.

9. Computers are writing classical music. The results, although not yet great, can be beautiful. Computers are writing novels. Not very good ones – but give them time. Then there's the recent paper describing the use of neural networks to allow a computer to transform a photograph into a painting in the style of one of the great masters.

10. Champions of AI look forward to the day when computers will fall in love and have their hearts broken, wonder about their place in the universe, and perhaps begin to resist their role as slaves to humans. Champions of humanity keep marking barriers and say that they have found the one the machines will never cross. But the circles are getting smaller.
